# Could it fit across the road? (green tractor + green front‑end loader, ~0:51–1:11)

## The scene I am talking about

The relevant shot runs from about **00:51 to 00:11:11 (i.e. 0:51–1:11)**. The camera
is standing on the raised, cobbled pavement on the left‑hand side of a narrow
two‑lane street in Rouen (farmers' Confédération Paysanne protest at the
Préfecture). Coming towards the camera are:

* a **green Fendt tractor** (a 700‑series Vario, red wheel rims) in the near,
  left‑hand lane, and
* a **green John Deere tractor fitted with a green Stoll front‑end loader**
  (yellow rims, bucket raised with a load of straw/muck, yellow protest flag on
  the cab) in the other lane, slightly further back.

Each is dragging a **high‑sided green/teal farm tipping trailer** ("benne
agricole") with steel body panels and mesh/rail extensions on top; the one in
shot is loaded with bundles of reeds/brushwood that stick out over the top.
The two trailers are the same general type and size, so the conclusions below
hold whichever of the two machines you assign a given trailer to.

## How wide is the road closest to the camera?

I measured this from the frames around 00:55–00:57, where the Fendt (left lane)
and a white "TERRIER" panel van (right lane) are side by side and between them
practically fill the carriageway:

* Fendt over the rear tyres ≈ **2.5 m** → 161 px in frame
* Van body ≈ **1.9 m** → 117 px in frame (consistent scale, ≈ 62 px per metre)
* Kerb to kerb at that same depth ≈ 364 px

That gives a carriageway of roughly **6 m, call it 5.5–6.5 m** – two narrow
~3 m lanes, which is exactly what you see: the tractor and the van only just
pass each other, with about half a metre between them and less than half a
metre to each kerb. (If you counted the pavements as well the street is more
like 12–14 m building to building, but "the road" – the asphalt between the
kerbs – is about 6 m.)

## 1. The trailer on its own, turned perpendicular to the road

**Just barely – it is essentially an exact fit, with nothing to spare, and its
drawbar would very likely overhang the kerb.**

That trailer is a tandem‑axle tipping trailer of the 12–16 tonne class:
about 2.4–2.5 m wide, with a body roughly **5.5 m long**, and an overall length
including the A‑frame drawbar and hitch eye of about **7 m** (6.5–7.5 m).

So turned broadside across a ~6 m road:

* the **body alone** (≈5.5 m) would sit inside the kerbs with only a few tens of
  centimetres to spare;
* measured **overall, drawbar included** (≈7 m), it is about a metre too long –
  the drawbar would stick up over the kerb onto the footway.

In short: the trailer is very nearly as long as the road is wide. It would span
the road almost exactly kerb‑to‑kerb and would completely block it; whether you
call that "fitting" depends on whether you count the drawbar.

## 2. The front‑end loader **and** its trailer together, turned perpendicular

**No – not even close.**

The John Deere is a big six‑cylinder machine: I measured its wheelbase at about
2.75 m against its 600/85R38 rear tyres (~2.0 m tall), which makes the tractor
about **5 m long**, and about **5.5–6.5 m** with the front loader fitted,
depending on where the bucket is. Hitched to the ~7 m trailer, the complete rig
is roughly **12–13 m long**.

That is about **twice the width of the road**. Laid across it, roughly 3 m
would stick out past each kerb – it would cover both pavements as well as the
whole carriageway, and would very nearly reach the building fronts on either
side. It does not fit.

**No – also about double the available width.**

The Fendt is around **4.9–5.5 m** long (a 716 Vario is about 4.9 m, a bit more
with front weights). With the ~7 m trailer behind it the outfit is roughly
**11.5–12.5 m** long – again close to twice the ~6 m carriageway, so it would
overhang by around 3 m at each end. It does not fit either.

## Summary

| Turned broadside across the ~6 m road | Fits? |
|---|---|
| Trailer alone (~7 m overall, ~5.5 m body) | Only just / marginally – body yes, drawbar overhangs. It would span the full road width with no clearance. |
| Front‑end loader + its trailer (~12–13 m) | **No** – roughly double the road width |
| Tractor + its trailer (~11.5–12.5 m) | **No** – roughly double the road width |

A useful sanity check visible in the video itself: either tractor **on its own**
(about 5 m) would fit across this road with roughly a metre to spare – which is
why one trailer alone is right on the borderline, and why adding a tractor in
front of it puts the combination hopelessly over.

All figures are photogrammetric estimates from a 854×480 video and carry maybe
±10–15 % uncertainty; that is easily enough precision to settle questions 2 and
